paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few subjects divide parents, teachers and students as much as homework. Some countries, such as Finland, give very little, and their students still perform well in international tests. Others, like South Korea, expect several hours every night. So who is right?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Supporters of homework make three main points. First, it gives students extra practice, and practice is how skills improve. Second, it teaches them to work alone and to manage their time. Third, it allows parents to see what their children are learning. A study of schools in several countries found that homework helped older students more than younger ones.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics answer that for young children homework brings little benefit and a lot of stress. After a long school day, children need time to play, rest and be with their families. Research also suggests that long hours of homework can lead to poor sleep. Another problem is fairness: a student with a quiet room and a helpful parent has a big advantage over a student who has neither.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In my opinion, the best approach lies in the middle. Homework should be short for younger students, perhaps ten minutes for each year of age, and it should be more interesting than simply repeating what was done in class. For teenagers, longer tasks make sense, but teachers should talk to each other so that students do not receive three big assignments on the same night.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Finally, schools could offer a homework club, where students can work in a quiet room with help available. This would reduce the unfairness and give everyone a chance to succeed. Homework is not good or bad in itself; what matters is how much is given, and why.
